claims.text: Pulumi maintains a documented provider support policy that specifies how long Pulumi maintains each provider major version.
Some Pulumi providers receive long-term security updates while others do not, per Pulumi's provider support policy.
Pulumi's provider support policy is documented at the page /docs/support/provider-support-policy/.
Pulumi does not automatically rollback changes made during an update if an error or failure occurs.
If an error or failure occurs during a Pulumi update, Pulumi completes any pending operations currently in progress and then exits and reports the error or failure.

To accomplish a manual rollback after a failed Pulumi deployment, you revert the code and configuration changes of the failed deployment and run `pulumi up` to update your infrastructure to its previous state.
Pulumi does not automatically query your cloud provider's live state before running `pulumi up` or `pulumi preview`.
Pulumi compares the desired state declared in your program against the last recorded state to determine what changes to make.
Refreshing state requires a round-trip to your cloud provider for every resource in a Pulumi stack.
The round-trip required for refreshing state adds significant latency, especially for large Pulumi stacks.
Running `pulumi refresh` synchronizes Pulumi's recorded state with the actual state of your cloud resources.
You can refresh and apply your desired state in a single step using `pulumi up --refresh`.
Pulumi Cloud provides built-in drift detection for automated drift detection and remediation on a schedule.
The Pulumi documentation page 'Refreshing state' (/docs/iac/concepts/state-and-backends/#refreshing-state) contains a detailed explanation of refresh behavior.
Pulumi resources have different logical names and physical names.
A Pulumi resource's logical name is how the resource is known to Pulumi and is part of the auto-assigned resource URN.
A Pulumi resource's physical name is how the resource is known to the cloud provider.
A Pulumi resource's logical name only needs to be unique within a stack.
A Pulumi resource's physical name typically needs to be unique within a certain scope, sometimes even globally.
Pulumi automatically creates each resource's physical name by combining the logical name with a random suffix appended afterwards.
Pulumi's auto-naming approach helps ensure that many logical Pulumi resources and stacks can be stood up side-by-side without conflicting.
Pulumi's auto-naming approach helps Pulumi replace resources with less downtime by creating the replacement before deleting the old resource.
With Pulumi's default auto-naming, a resource's physical name will typically look like `my-bucket-d7c2fa0` instead of `my-bucket`.
You can disable Pulumi's auto-naming on a per-resource basis.

Disabling Pulumi's auto-naming on a per-resource basis lets you have precise physical names without random suffixes, but means you lose the reduced-conflict and reduced-downtime-replacement benefits of auto-naming.
You can use project or stack configuration to customize or disable Pulumi's auto-naming globally, per provider, or per resource type.
Pulumi provides primitives so you can enforce that your secrets are stored in a secure manner in the CLI, state file, and Pulumi Cloud.
During a Pulumi update, secrets are decrypted in memory and visible to your Pulumi program.
You may pass `--secret` to `pulumi config set` to cause a configuration value to be encrypted so it can be safely persisted in `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml`.
For every stack, Pulumi Cloud manages a unique encryption key which it uses to encrypt secrets for that stack.
Pulumi Cloud's per-stack secrets encryption is configurable to use your own custom secrets provider.

Because a different encryption key is used for each stack, encrypting the same value across two different stacks leads to different encrypted strings being stored in the `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml` files.
You cannot copy an encrypted secret value from one `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml` file to another using a text editor.
To copy a secret value between stack config files, you must use `pulumi config set`.
When you run a preview, update, or destroy, Pulumi decrypts secret configuration data.
During execution of a Pulumi deployment, decrypted secret data is plain text and any part of your Pulumi program may access it using the Pulumi config object.
Pulumi does not use the Terraform engine in any way.
Some Pulumi providers use the open-source Terraform schemas in order to know what resources and parameters are available, and to determine the return and response attributes.
Pulumi native providers are mapped directly to the cloud provider APIs and do not use Terraform schemas.
Pulumi is a declarative tool that uses imperative languages to define your end state.
Pulumi uses strongly typed languages with programming languages that support IntelliSense and the Language Server Protocol.
Pulumi experimental features are always opt-in, requiring explicit enabling via a flag, command, or environment variable such as `PULUMI_EXPERIMENTAL=true`.
Pulumi experimental features are not necessarily supported and can change or be removed at any time without a deprecation cycle.
When a Pulumi experimental feature proves valuable, Pulumi invests in stabilizing it and promoting it to general availability.
Pulumi focuses on actively supporting the latest released major version of the providers it maintains.
For a set of widely used providers, Pulumi ships security updates for the previous major version for up to a year, or until the next major version is released, whichever comes first.
The provider support policy page (/docs/support/provider-support-policy/) lists the covered providers and what a long-term support release contains.
Older major versions of Pulumi providers receive no patches at all.
You can find the current version for all providers maintained by Pulumi in the Pulumi Registry.
When a major version of a Pulumi provider is released, that is a signal to begin planning a provider version update.
Major versions of Pulumi providers typically include significant changes such as deprecations, new resources, and new functionality, which may require additional migration steps.
Pulumi recommends that, at least quarterly, you consider updating to the latest minor version on the current major and review provider release notes.
Minor versions of Pulumi providers typically include new resources and features, as well as performance improvements and bug fixes, without introducing breaking changes.
Using the tilde operator in npm (e.g., ~1.2.3) allows patch updates on the current minor version while pinning the major and minor version.
Patch versions of Pulumi providers are primarily for bug fixes and security updates and are designed to be fully backward compatible.
Pulumi recommends never being 2 major versions behind on a provider, because jumping multiple major versions is inadvisable due to the number of potential breaking changes.
Each major version of a Pulumi provider includes migration logic to smooth the upgrade from the immediately previous major version.
Migration logic in Pulumi providers does not always work across multiple major versions.
The 'Provider support policy' page is located at /docs/support/provider-support-policy/.
Pulumi actively maintains the latest released major version of every provider it publishes.
For a set of widely used providers, Pulumi ships security updates for the previous major version for up to 12 months, or until the next major version is released, whichever comes first.
Pulumi's AWS provider is on the current list of providers that receive long-term support updates on eligible older versions.
Pulumi's Azure Classic provider is on the current list of providers that receive long-term support updates on eligible older versions.
Pulumi's Azure Native provider is on the current list of providers that receive long-term support updates on eligible older versions.
Pulumi's Azure AD provider is on the current list of providers that receive long-term support updates on eligible older versions.
Pulumi's Command provider is on the current list of providers that receive long-term support updates on eligible older versions.
Pulumi's Docker Build provider is on the current list of providers that receive long-term support updates on eligible older versions.
Pulumi's GCP provider is on the current list of providers that receive long-term support updates on eligible older versions.
Pulumi's Kubernetes provider is on the current list of providers that receive long-term support updates on eligible older versions.
Pulumi's TLS provider is on the current list of providers that receive long-term support updates on eligible older versions.
Pulumi's Vault provider is on the current list of providers that receive long-term support updates on eligible older versions.

The Pulumi provider long-term support (LTS) branch ships fixes for High/Critical CVEs affecting the provider's code or its direct dependencies.
The Pulumi provider long-term support (LTS) branch ships fixes for broken internal infrastructure on the LTS branch needed to ship CVE security patches.
A Pulumi provider LTS release does not contain new upstream API versions.
A Pulumi provider LTS release does not contain new resources or new resource properties.
A Pulumi provider LTS release does not contain performance improvements.
A Pulumi provider LTS release does not contain non-security bug fixes.
A Pulumi provider LTS release does not contain compatibility updates for newer versions of language runtimes.
Pulumi providers are compatible with the version of the Pulumi engine they were frozen at, unless otherwise prompted via security fixes.
Exactly one long-term support major version exists per Pulumi provider at any time.
When a Pulumi provider's major version N+1 ships, it becomes the new current major (N), and the old N becomes the new long-term support (LTS) major.
When a new Pulumi provider major version ships, the old long-term support major reaches end of life on the same day, regardless of how much of its 12-month window remained.
Within a Pulumi provider's long-term support major version, only the latest minor version receives patches, and earlier minors are frozen.
Pulumi LTS provider releases are available through the same standard package registries as current-major releases, but are tagged differently.
Pulumi recommends that customers pin to a specific provider major version.
Customers who pin a Pulumi provider to a specific major version automatically receive patch releases as they ship.
At any time, exactly one major version of a covered Pulumi provider is the LTS version.
Older major versions of a covered Pulumi provider receive no patches.
The current major (N) version of a Pulumi provider receives support until N+1 ships.
The current major (N) version of a Pulumi provider ships new features, new resources, bug fixes, security patches, dependency upgrades, and new upstream API versions.
The long-term support (N−1) major version of a Pulumi provider is supported for up to 12 months from N's release, or until N+1 ships.
The long-term support (N−1) major version of a Pulumi provider ships only security updates in the provider's code or its direct dependencies.
Pulumi provider major versions N−2 and older are end of life and are not supported and will not receive updates.
A page titled "Best practices for maintaining provider versions" exists at /docs/support/faq/infrastructure/#what-are-the-best-practices-for-maintaining-provider-versions.
The Pulumi Registry page exists at /registry/.
A "Getting support" page exists at /docs/support/getting-support/.
